The story is children of Typography, so it reads as typeset text at the 34rem measure. /** A folly in an arched frame with its caption, side by side from 30rem and stacked below that. */ export function ArchFigure({ seed, label, caption, }: { seed: string /** What the drawing shows, for assistive technology. */ label: string caption: ReactNode }) { return ( ) } /** A sentence lifted from the text, large in the extended sans under a sparkle, with who said it in the capitals. */ export function PullQuote({ children, cite, }: { children: ReactNode cite?: string }) { return ( ) } export function SaturnStory() { return ( <>

Saturn passed opposition last month, when it sat exactly opposite the Sun: rising at sunset, highest in the south around midnight, setting at dawn. It is still up from dusk until the small hours, and it will not be this close or this bright again until next autumn.

Opposition comes round every year and thirteen days, as the Earth overtakes Saturn on the inside track. What makes this season worth a cold night on the deck is the rings. Last year they were edge on to us, a thin line through the planet that most visitors took for a scratch on the eyepiece. Now they are tilting open again, a little more every month.

Why the rings grew brighter

Around opposition the Sun was directly behind us, so we saw the ring particles fully lit with no shadows between them. For a few nights the rings brightened more than the planet did, an effect astronomers call opposition surge. It is the same reason a field of frost glitters hardest when the Sun is at your back.

For a few nights the rings outshone the planet they circle.

Seeing it from the deck

The Zeiss refractor shows the rings, the Cassini division in them when the air is steady, and Titan as a small orange star off to one side. On a good night you can make out the cloud belts across the ball, and the shadow the planet throws on the rings behind it.

  • Look south-east from 19:00; Saturn is the steady yellow light.
  • Give your eyes ten minutes in the dark before the eyepiece.
  • Steady air matters more than a clear sky; we post the seeing.

The deck is open every clear night this month from dusk. Members book four weeks ahead; everyone else can come to the door and wait for a turn, which on a Saturday rarely takes more than twenty minutes.
